title: Pan de Muerto
subtitle: Mexican Day of the Dead sweet orange bread
excerpt: Pan de muerto is a soft, enriched bread scented with orange zest and aniseed, baked for Dia de los Muertos. It takes around 3 hours including rising time but is not difficult to make. One large loaf serves 8.
sourceNotes: Pan de muerto is baked in the weeks leading up to Dia de los Muertos on 1 and 2 November. The round loaf is decorated with dough strips shaped to represent bones and a small sphere for a skull. It is placed on ofrendas (altars) to honour the dead and is eaten by families during the celebration.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooled, unglazed loaf for up to 1 month. Defrost at room temperature and glaze just before serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the day before and keep covered at room temperature. Warm briefly in a low oven before serving.

content.text: This recipe makes one large loaf serving 8 and takes about 3 hours and 5 minutes in total, including 2 hours of rising time. The dough is enriched with eggs, butter and orange zest, which gives it a soft, slightly sweet crumb. The 7g of fast-action yeast is dissolved in 120ml warm milk before mixing into the flour.

The dough is stickier than a standard bread dough because of the eggs and butter. Resist adding extra flour when kneading. A slightly tacky dough produces a softer crumb. After shaping, reserve a small portion of dough for the bone decorations before the second rise. Glaze the finished loaf with 40g of melted butter while still hot from the oven, then roll it in caster sugar immediately so the sugar sticks.
Warm 120ml of milk to around 38C. It should feel warm but not hot to the touch. Stir in the 7g sachet of fast-action yeast and leave for 5 minutes until slightly foamy.
Place the flour and 100g caster sugar in a large bowl. Add the zest of 2 oranges and the 1 teaspoon of aniseed if using. Mix briefly to combine.

Make a well in the centre. Pour in the yeast mixture, then add the 3 eggs and the 80g softened butter, cut into small pieces. Mix to a rough dough, then turn out and knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough will be slightly sticky. Do not add more flour.
Lightly oil a large bowl. Place the dough inside, cover with a clean tea towel and leave to rise in a warm spot for 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes, until doubled in size.
Knock the dough back gently. Pull off a piece roughly the size of a small orange for the decorations. Shape the main dough into a smooth round ball and place on a lined baking tray.

Divide the reserved dough into 5 small pieces. Roll 4 pieces into long, thin sausages to represent bones. Roll the 5th piece into a small ball for the skull. Lay the bone strips over the top of the loaf in a cross and place the ball in the centre. Press them gently to secure.
Cover loosely and leave to rise for a further 30 to 45 minutes until noticeably puffed. Preheat the oven to 180C.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden brown and hollow-sounding when tapped underneath. If the top colours too quickly, lay a piece of foil loosely over it after 20 minutes.

While the loaf is still hot, brush the entire surface with the 40g melted butter. Sprinkle generously with caster sugar so it sticks to the butter and forms a lightly sweet crust. Leave to cool on a wire rack for at least 20 minutes before slicing.

attrs.symptom: The dough does not rise after an hour
attrs.cause: The yeast was killed by milk that was too hot, or the yeast was old and inactive
attrs.fix: Check the milk temperature. It should feel warm but comfortable on your wrist, around 38C. Water above 45C kills yeast. If the yeast did not foam after 5 minutes in warm milk, discard it and use a fresh sachet. Proof the yeast before adding to the dough.

attrs.symptom: The bone decorations crack or fall off during baking
attrs.cause: The decoration pieces were too dry or not attached firmly before the second rise
attrs.fix: Dampen the underside of each bone strip with a little water before pressing it onto the loaf. Let the decorations rise with the loaf for the full second rise so they bond to the surface before baking. Do not press them on just before the oven.

attrs.symptom: The crumb is dense and heavy rather than soft and open
attrs.cause: The dough was not kneaded long enough or did not have enough time to rise fully
attrs.fix: Knead for the full 10 minutes to develop gluten. The dough should pass the windowpane test, stretching thin without tearing. Make sure the first rise has truly doubled the volume before shaping. A cold kitchen slows yeast significantly, so move the bowl somewhere warmer if needed.

content.text: Pan de muerto is baked across Mexico in October and early November. Bakeries start making it weeks before Dia de los Muertos. Families place it on ofrendas alongside photographs, candles and marigolds. It is soft and lightly sweet, scented with orange and anise. After the celebrations, it is eaten at home with coffee or hot chocolate.
